subject: physics
title: Changes in momentum and safety features
key_idea: (Higher tier) Force equals the rate of change of momentum. Safety features such as air bags and crash mats make the stopping time longer. The momentum changes at a lower rate, so the force on a person is smaller.

sections.heading: Force and rate of change of momentum

blocks.text: (Higher tier) When a force acts on a moving object, its momentum changes. This section links force, acceleration and change in momentum.

items: Newton's second law gives force = mass × acceleration, F = m a.
Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken, a = (v − u) ÷ t.
Putting these together gives force = change in momentum ÷ time.

blocks.label: Force and change in momentum
blocks.formula: F = m Δv ÷ Δt   (also written F = (m v − m u) ÷ t)
where: F is the force, in newtons, N
m is the mass, in kilograms, kg
Δv is the change in velocity, in metres per second, m/s (v is the final velocity and u is the initial velocity)
Δt is the time taken, in seconds, s

blocks.text: The term m Δv is the change in momentum. So the force equals the rate of change of momentum.

items: Convert times to seconds first. For example, 180 ms = 0.18 s.
If an object reverses direction, add the two velocities to find the change. A ball arriving at 8.2 m/s and leaving at 15 m/s the other way has Δv = 8.2 + 15 = 23.2 m/s.

sections.heading: How safety features reduce the force

blocks.text: (Higher tier) Safety features do not remove the change in momentum. They spread it over a longer time.

items: Air bags and seat belts in cars.
Crash mats in a gym.
Cycle helmets.
Cushioned surfaces in playgrounds.
Crumple zones, flexible bumpers and protective pads.

items.text: The person's momentum still has to fall to zero.
The safety feature increases the time taken to stop.
The rate of change of momentum decreases, so the deceleration is less.
The force on the person is reduced, so there is less risk of injury.

items: Doubling the stopping time halves the force.
A longer stopping time also reduces the deceleration.
Safety features increase the time taken to stop.
The change in momentum is the same, so the rate of change decreases and the force is reduced.
A smaller force means less risk of injury.

checks.q: State the equation that links force to change in momentum.
checks.a: Force = change in momentum ÷ time (F = mΔv ÷ Δt).

checks.q: Explain how an air bag reduces the chance of injury to a driver.
checks.a: It increases the time taken for the driver to stop. So the rate of change of momentum decreases, which means the force on the driver is reduced.

checks.q: A ball of mass 0.50 kg stops in 0.20 s from a velocity of 6.0 m/s. Calculate the average force.

worked_example.question:
Cars have air bags that inflate to protect the driver if the car stops very suddenly.

Explain how air bags reduce the chance of injury to the driver.
answer_points: The air bag increases the time taken for the driver to come to a stop.
So the rate of change of momentum decreases (the deceleration of the driver is less).
So the force on the driver is reduced.
worked_example.tip: For the first two marks, the change of momentum is the same but over a greater time is also allowed.

worked_example.question:
A gymnast lands on a mat and comes to rest.

The gymnast has a mass of 53 kg.

The gymnast lands on the mat with a velocity of 4.0 m/s.

The average force exerted by the mat on the gymnast is 3500 N.

Calculate the time taken for the gymnast to come to rest.

Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.

Use the equation
force = change in momentum / time
answer_points: 3500 = 53 × 4 ÷ time (the change in momentum is 53 × 4 = 212 kg m/s)
worked_example.tip: One mark for the substitution or rearrangement, one for the evaluation and one for rounding the calculated value to 2 significant figures.

worked_example.question:
A van travels along a road at a constant speed.

If the van crashes, the time taken to stop is much smaller.

Explain why this is dangerous for the people in the van.
answer_points: The acceleration will increase, and force = mass × acceleration, so there is a greater force on the occupants.
This could lead to injury of the people in the van.
worked_example.tip: Any two points score the 2 marks. Force = rate of change of momentum is also allowed.

worked_example.question:
The concrete floor under a seesaw is replaced with a rubber floor. A child falls from the seesaw and experiences an impulse when they hit the floor.

Explain how the rubber floor reduces injury to the child. Use ideas about impulse, force, momentum and time in your answer.
answer_points: The change in momentum (the impulse) is the same on both floors.
The change in momentum takes place over a longer time on the rubber floor.
force = change in momentum ÷ time, so the force on the child is smaller and there is less injury.
worked_example.tip: Any three of these points score the three marks.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Impulse is the force multiplied by the time for which it acts. It equals the change in momentum.

blocks.label: Impulse
where: impulse is in newton seconds (N s), the same as kg m/s.
F is the force in newtons (N).
Δt is the time for which the force acts in seconds (s).
Δ(mv) is the change in momentum in kg m/s.

items: Safety features give the same impulse over a longer time, so the force is smaller.
The resultant force is the change in momentum per unit time: F = Δp ÷ Δt.

worked_example.question:
A cricket player hits a ball with a bat. Before the ball is hit, it is moving to the left with a momentum of 4.2 kg m/s. The bat is in contact with the ball for 0.012 s. After the ball is hit, it moves to the right with a momentum of 6.7 kg m/s.

Calculate the mean force the bat exerts on the ball and state the direction of the force.
answer_points: The directions are opposite, so the change in momentum = 6.7 + 4.2 = 10.9 kg m/s
F = 10.9 ÷ 0.012 = 908 N, which is 910 N to 2 significant figures
The force is to the right.
